Lissa Skitol  

Joshua Hirsch has given me one more reason to explain why I hate Schindler's List. In his new book, Afterimage: Film, Trauma, and the Holocaust, he makes a significant contribution to the debate surrounding the value and effects of Holocaust films through a discussion of a group of films that are both symptoms and expressions of the personal and historical trauma wrought by Nazi Germany. Hirsch claims that the well-known documentaries Night and Fog (Resnais, 1955) and Shoah (Lanzmann, 1985) first established certain features of a post-traumatic cinema that were then adopted and developed in less well-known fictional movies such as The Pawnbroker (Lumet, 1965) and three by the Hungarian filmmaker István Szabó: Father (1966), Love Film (1970), and 25 Fireman Street (1973). These are distinguished from more contemporary Holocaust movies such as Schindler's List and Life is Beautiful, both for their rejection of classical realism (the intent to portray the way “it really was”) and for their ability to transmit the structure of trauma - the impossibility of assuming a past that invades and fractures the present - through their form and content.

Hirsch provides a fascinating analysis of how these films adopt symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder into the structure of cinematography, perhaps most evident through the use of the flashback as a device to interrupt rather than explain the narrative of a film. These films “formally repeat the traumatic structure of the experience of witnessing the events themselves” (p 3), as they all take place after the trauma of Nazism, which nevertheless invades their narratives and interrupts their linear continuity (in these films the present and the past always converge and obscure one another). Further, akin to traumatic recollection, which forces an individual to bear witness to the failure of memory and the inability to master the past, Hirsch draws attention to the fact that these films are self-conscious about the limits of representation and their failure to adequately depict the trauma of Nazism and the experience of those who suffer from its assault (p 44). He argues that this is expressed both directly (as in Night and Fog) and indirectly through conventions such as the abbreviated flashback which is seen but not perceived (as in The Pawnbroker) and a Holocaust film-within-the-film (as in Father).

Divided into two parts, Cultures of the Death Drive has a double project. First, Esther Sánchez-Pardo wants to foreground melancholia as fundamental to Melanie Klein's work. The focus here is naturally enough on the “depressive position,” that stage in which the child seeks to internalize the ambiguous objects that have given rise to its earlier anxieties, the chief of these objects being the mother's breast. This process may involve both mourning and melancholia. Mourning requires the successful internalization of a lost object in its “good” aspect, and thus is a positive act of possession in the very heart of loss. When that internalization fails, the result is melancholia. It fails because of an excess of aggression and anxiety directed toward the object, which is seen as “bad,” an annihilating force that reflects the child's own destructive impulses. This, according to Klein, is how the death drive manifests itself within the psyche. Yet the death drive is not only an internal dynamic but also an external, social one. Entire societies may exhibit aggression and anxiety toward whatever is felt to be outside them - whether these are different ideologies, or races, or sexualities. The resulting “cultures of the death drive” resonate with the primal melancholia, which may in any adult be intensely revived by later, social, events.

Editorial

Lynne Layton and Simon Clarke

Simon Clarke

Simon Clarke  

In this issue, we present a cluster of articles that take up the relation between psychoanalysis and film. The fields of cultural studies and film theory have been marked from their very beginnings by psychoanalysis: one has only to consider the groundbreaking work of Screen theorists in the 1970s and 1980s, who, influenced by Lacan and Althusser, exposed cinema as an ideological state apparatus (see Easthope (1983) for a review of this work). Laura Mulvey (1975), Stephen Heath (1981), Christian Metz (1982), and many others examined, for example, the ideological effects of standard Hollywood editing techniques, relations between spectators and spectacle, and the way subjects are interpellated into particular sexist, racist, and heterosexist subject positions. Both during and after the heyday of Screen theory, literary and film critics also drew on object relations, self psychology, and other versions of Lacanian theory to produce a large body of work about the relation between cultural representations, the institutions in which they emerge, and the formation and development of subjectivity. Janice Radway (1984), for example, created a paradigm for audience study that blended feminist psychoanalytic object relations with the ethnographic model developed by the Birmingham School. To mention just one more example, Žižek turns repeatedly to film and fiction to exemplify such Lacanian concepts as the Real (e.g., Žižek, 1991) and to point to the fantasmatic underpinnings of contemporary socio-political relations.

Each of the articles in this issue, as well as Jan Haaken's field note, further develops different strands of the rich and hybrid 30-something-year-old tradition of left-wing psychoanalytic cultural criticism. In “Lacan for Cinema Today: the Uncanny Pouvoir de la Vérité”, Fabio Vighi revisits Screen Theory's work on editing, suture, and the gaze, demonstrating the way that the Lacanian concept of the Real alters our understanding of these processes, and elucidating, as he does so, their political potential.

This article examines two approaches to the study of films from the perspective of psychoanalysis. The paper argues that the psychoanalytic “reading” of films - and other cultural objects - should at all times be aware not just of the conscious and unconscious meanings present in those films, but also of the way that the unconscious thoughts of the person who is “reading” the film may influence or re-direct any straightforward interpretation. The reading of films is thus a two-way affair: a reading may be directed towards a film, but the film will also be “giving something back.” The article thus examines two psychoanalytic “readings” of films, a first that does not take into account the two-way nature of psychoanalytic reading, and a second that does.

Howard Stein has long been one of the most astute and trenchant observers of the American cultural scene from a perspective informed by both cultural anthropology and psychoanalysis. If he is less well known than he deserves to be, this is in part because like anyone with a message that addresses the disavowed motives underlying contemporary social and cultural phenomena, he tells people precisely what they don't want to hear. But he occupies a unique and vital place on the current horizon, precisely because, like a voice crying out in the wilderness (in this case, from the heartland, Oklahoma City, where he is a Professor in the Department of Family and Preventative Medicine at the University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center), he so persistently draws our attention back to the dynamics that drive our actions and compel us to try to shield ourselves from direct knowledge of what we are up to. He writes from a position informed by tireless immersion as a participant-observer - with a greater-than-usual emphasis on the “participant” part - in the cultural processes and traumas that have scarred and shaped the psyche of America, especially Red State America, over the past couple of decades. Not only an academic scholar, he is a committed activist and public intellectual deeply engaged in the community life around him, whose writings bear the mark of lived experience with and involvement in the issues about which he writes.

Beneath the Crust of Culture is a collection of essays covering an array of subjects bound to interest anyone trying to make sense of contemporary American cultural phenomena, from the aftermath of 9/11 to matters in which Stein's more direct involvement gives him particular authority to speak, such as the Oklahoma City bombing of 1995, the execution of its perpetrator, Timothy McVeigh, the Columbine High School massacre across the border in Colorado, and, as a backdrop, the decades long juggernaut of downsizing, outsourcing, reengineering, RIFing and other euphemisms for massive layoffs of employees in big corporations, not least in the very medical organizations in which Stein himself works.

The task of writing an introduction to the work of Slavoj Žižek brings with it a unique set of challenges. One such challenge lies in the fact that Žižek is a thinker less concerned with devising an original set of concepts than toying with an elusive Hegelian-Marxist-Lacanian assemblage of ideas. As such, it is often less an introduction to Žižek that we need than an introduction to the formidable edifice of ideas that forms the foundation of his various critical speculations. That said, there has been no shortage of ostensibly “critical” introductions to Žižek. At least two have preceded Parker's treatment; these titles provide the immediate benchmarks against which his text should be assessed.

Kay's (2003) Žižek: A Critical Introduction succeeds admirably in connecting Žižek's cultural and political criticism to the vocabulary of Lacanian psychoanalysis, and manages to do so without surrendering the complexity of the material. Her consideration of Žižek's politics is, unfortunately, toothless by comparison. Slavoj Žižek by Tony Myers (2003) provides the quick-fix: a succession of rapid illuminations that helps one grasp Žižek in a series of “eureka” moments which, alas, dissipate all too quickly in the lack of a more sustained engagement.

The first obvious difference between Parker's text and these two earlier books is that Parker provides a thorough historical contextualization - in the form of a discussion of the rise and decomposition of the Yugoslav state - of the conditions of (im)possibility from which Žižek's thought emerges. (In speaking of “conditions of impossibility” Parker intends to draw our attention to the fact that concepts are sometimes utilized precisely so as to render points of apparent historical impossibility comprehensible.) The problem with this attempt at contextualization is twofold. The compression of analysis required to put Žižek's political thought in dialogue with the formation of Slovenia is, firstly, difficult to adequately accommodate in 25 pages. cinema; fantasy; history; masculinities; trauma

This paper uses psychoanalytic and cultural theories to explore contemporary shifts in hegemonic masculinities through a discussion of their representation in mainstream cinema. By interrogating the uses made in cinema of ideas around history, trauma and mythology, we suggest that masculinity has been undergoing a stage of cultural transition towards new modes of masculinity that challenge the rigidities of images in previous decades. The political potential of such images may also, however, be ultimately reined in by the insistence of the hegemonic set of discourses around representation. However, by drawing on psychoanalytic explanations of trauma, gender and cultural fantasy, we show that these cinematic representations of masculinity are often highly complex, ambiguous and transitional, and, as such, may lie somewhere in between overly defensive narcissistic modes of masculinity and those which are more fluid and open to change. In the end, we settle on the importance of seeing representations of masculinities as forming a continuum between these positions. While foregrounding that ambiguity, we explore both the potentially positive and negative implications for the kind of identifications and affective responses that are opened up for the spectator, and the readings that are created as a result.

Two legacies from the early 20th century continue to goad critical thought: W.E.B. Dubois' famously articulated “problem of the color line” and Sigmund Freud's equally pressing, if somewhat more baffled complaint, “What does a woman want?” Taking on the ambitious task of thinking these two issues together, Jean Wyatt's Risking Difference: Identification, Race and Community in Contemporary Fiction and Feminism is the latest in a series of books that considers the costs of disavowing envy, idealization, and oppression in communities of difference.

Recent studies that, like Risking Difference, use feminism, race theory and psychoanalysis to interpret the difficulties of community in contemporary society include Female Subjects in Black and White: Race, Psychoanalysis, and Feminism, edited by Elizabeth Abel, Barbara Christian, and Helene Moglen (1997), Barbara Johnson's Literature, Psychoanalysis, Race and Gender: The Feminist Difference (1998), Claudia Tate's Psychoanalysis and Black Novels: Desire and Protocols of Race (1998), and several essays in The Psychoanalysis of Race, edited by Christopher Lane (1998). Wyatt's book stands out, however, in its focus on the Freudian theories - and their Lacanian revisions - of identification. Identification, Wyatt explains early on, “captures the global nature of the desire to become the other, to replace the other - a desire that … undergirds everyday structures of feeling like envy and idealization” (p 1). Wyatt emphasizes the tension inherent in desiring to become and/or replace the other: Despite the value we find in the other, a value that might unite us, the desire for identification also risks “reducing the other to an empty form,” thus denying her subjectivity (p 3). Wyatt's book consistently engages these dueling forces, ultimately calling for “some rupture of the shared assumptions - and the assumption of sharing - in a community”: a rupture that has the potential to break “the communal drive toward assimilation of difference” (p 185). This rupture, Wyatt argues (following June Jordan), will break through the polite surfaces of white and black feminist discourse and simultaneously prevent appropriation on the side of white feminists and silent acquiescence on the side of black feminists (pp 184-185).

Pink Ribbons and Bad Girls of Breast Cancer

Randy Milden

Randy Milden

1129 Curtis St., Albany CA 94706, USA
E-mail: rmilden@pacbell.net

Randy Milden   Writer and educator living in the San Francisco Bay Area.
breast cancer; race for cure; treatment; survivors; popularization

For many women, twenty five years ago, breast cancer was a shameful secret. Diagnosed with breast cancer in 1979, my mother chose a crack-of-dawn appointment for her daily radiation therapy. Her goal: to drive the hour to and from Boston and be back on the golf course in time to play nine holes, so nobody would suspect that she was sick.

Today, breast cancer has such a public face that The Onion ran a satirical story entitled “March Named Breast Cancer Obliviousness Month” (The Onion, 2002). It sometimes seems hard to walk a city block without encountering a parade of fund-raising posters for breast cancer research, featuring radiant women identified as breast cancer survivors. But my perception may be skewed. I was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2002.

Most observers concur that the popularization of breast cancer has mitigated the stigma once associated with it. But in a widely cited essay written in response to her own breast cancer diagnosis, Barbara Ehrenreich (2001) argues that the contemporary culture of the disease is corrupted by patriarchal values and corporate self-interest.

Ehrenreich trains a critical lens on the Susan G. Komen Foundation, an organization at the forefront of the transformation of breast cancer culture. Komen collaborates with mainstream scientists, clinicians, and businesses, raising money for breast cancer research and promoting early detection.

The writings of Slavoj Žižek have a disorienting effect on readers, and attempts to understand and utilize his ideas in cultural theory have often come to grief. One way into an interpretation of what Žižek is up to is to trace the cultural-political interventions of some fellow travellers still active in the production and disturbance of our ideological enjoyment. This commentary follows some of the contours of the landscape of Slovenian theory.

Transforming Mourning: Psychoanalytic Paradigms for Change in the Writing Classroom

I know that there is such anguish in you that you cannot say a single word.

(Akhmatova, 1921, transl. Kenyon, 1999, p 12)

New knowledge is an acquisition of meaning that facilitates growth, but it also comes with the price of de-acquisition of old knowledge. Change is a process that has its gains and losses. A psychoanalytic approach to writing classrooms is a pedagogy that seeks not only to expedite personal and social transformation for the betterment of the individual and his or her society, but also to examine and evaluate the meanings individuals attach to personal identity and culture. All teachers of writing can gain from an understanding of empathy, a concept not discussed frequently enough in composition theory or literary theory, for that matter. A better understanding of empathy in personal writing classes that encourage self-disclosure of sometimes difficult and painful material can lead to more self-awareness on the teacher's part, and therefore more effective teaching.

Importing psychoanalytic theory into the writing classroom is not only a challenging, but a complex task in light of postmodernist ethics. Since the 1980s, cultural criticism has questioned the veracity of psychoanalytic interpretation, arguing that only historical criticism can investigate the transformative possibilities of a cultural artifact by exposing hidden ideologies or suppressed voices within that cultural and historical moment. However, as Mark Bracher has pointed out, “identifying forms of power in the past does not necessarily tell us anything about how oppression and injustice are operating in the present, and even if it does tell us something about oppression and injustice in the present, that knowledge by itself does not necessarily change things for the better” (Bracher, 1993, p 7). Bracher's existential claim is not in the direction of doing away with historical interpretation; on the contrary, he wishes to bring history into a present moment in which social and cultural change is possible.

Todd McGowan

Todd McGowan

Burlington, Vermont

Todd McGowan  

When we think about history in the aftermath of the 20th century, we must inevitably think about trauma. To construct a contemporary philosophy of history is in some way to construct a philosophy of engaging trauma because the historical events that have the deepest claim on us as thinkers of history are traumatic. If we fail to grasp adequately the traumatic events of history, we perpetuate the trauma or, at least, do nothing to extirpate it. This is what Theodor Adorno (1992) suggests in Negative Dialectics when he claims that “a new categorical imperative has been imposed by Hitler upon unfree mankind: to arrange their thoughts and actions so that Auschwitz will not repeat itself, so that nothing similar will happen” (p 365). The problem is, however, that to think about history is also to theorize about it, and to approach history theoretically is to miss its traumatic dimension and thus to violate Adorno's “new categorical imperative.”

A theoretical approach places trauma of history within a meaningful framework, and this activity necessarily dissolves the nonsensical status of trauma. Trauma is always nonsensical; it is traumatic precisely because we can't render it sensible within a universe of meaning. It is Real in the sense that it resists symbolization absolutely, and we avoid it because it would reveal the truth of our existence. Hence, any effort to render the trauma of history through a theoretical understanding must be doomed to failure, insofar as apprehending the trauma forces it to signify and breaks down its resistance to sense.

But as Walter Davis argues in Deracination, there is a way out of this dilemma. In contrast to theorizing, aesthetic experience allows us to engage history in a way adequate to the experience of it. This is because aesthetic experience enables us to engage trauma without turning away from it or rendering it significant. The truth of history is traumatic, and aesthetic experience renders this trauma approachable. But aesthetic experience cannot theorize itself; it cannot transform itself into a coherent way of approaching history. For that, one must have a theory. In Deracination, Davis (2001) aims to construct a theory that incorporates aesthetic experience into a framework that engages trauma without subjecting it to signification.

gender; science studies; philosophy of science; Lacan

This essay enjoins Lacanian psychoanalysis to address a recurrent question in the philosophy of science regarding the role of gender (or perhaps other social categories) in the production of objective knowledge. Are social categories “merely empirical” and thus mitigated by the formal procedures of scientific investigation or is gender somehow implicated in the constitution of knowledge itself? Evelyn Fox Keller, in her monumentally influential work on gender and science, makes the case for a constitutive effect. This essay, using data from a year-long study of science labs and the concepts of Lacan, attempts to further Fox Keller's project by substituting object relations and the categories one thus has at one's disposal with an understanding of the structural effects of language (as limitation and the introduction of difference) as these are graphed on to embodied being, giving forms of what culture reveres as sexual difference - the phallic one vs the Other. Implications for thinking gender in science are suggested and those for the daily operations of research labs are also noted.

Nouri Gana  

Peter Homans' Symbolic Loss is an exemplary introduction to the complexities of the question of mourning in contemporary culture. In his introduction to this wide-ranging 10-essay collection, Homans distinguishes between grief (the emotional pain triggered by the loss of a love object) and mourning (the cultural and symbolic containment of grief by community-wide solidarity), and traces the decline of mourning practices back to, among other factors, the modernization of social life, the rise of psychoanalysis, as well as the breakup and dispersal of community into the carefully discriminated spheres of the private and the public. With no visible community to fall upon, the burden of mourning has fallen on the individual and therefore given rise to what Homans calls, in a very suggestive phrase, “mourning without mourning practices” (p 9). The bulk of Symbolic Loss is a sustained examination of the shaping forces of mourning in four representative fields (literature, history, architecture, psychology) of this new cultural paradigm of mourning practices.

The first part of Symbolic Loss brings together a cluster of three essays on American and African-American literature and music. Mitchell Breitwiser's “Fitzgerald, Kerouac, and the Puzzle of Inherited Mourning” is a compelling foray into the transgenerational commerce of losses from parent to child. Drawing on Nicolas Abraham and Maria Torok's book The Shell and the Kernel, Breitwiser pieces together the phantomatic demarcations of other people's experiences of loss that ripple through Fitzgerald's and Kerouac's works.

psychoanalytic cultural theory; drag performance; queer theory; female impersonation; video ethnography; humor

As it has migrated from gay culture to mainstream entertainment, drag performance has generated considerable controversy among queer theorists. Some theorists argue that drag reinforces binary categories of sex and gender by positioning itself as the boundary-defining Other - as the simulated act that preserves the fantasy of the genuine article. Judith Butler, among others, has countered that drag performance subverts the stability of gender as a social category, bringing into view illusory distinctions between masculine and feminine. In describing a documentary video project on the social psychology of drag performance, this field report takes up the question of what makes drag performance funny, and who or what pays the price of the joke.

reality television; Lacan; psychoanalysis; desire; perversity

This essay argues from a Lacanian perspective as to why “reality television” has become so pervasive in postmodern consumerist society. Against the widely held claim that such reality programming is democratically therapeutic in its effects to provide citizens a public forum to be seen and heard, another thesis is presented: such television programs reinforce the very perversity they claim to cure. By focusing on the film, The Truman Show, this perversity is exposed through a Lacanian reading of its redemptive fantasy. The essay ends with the question of impossibility: to what extent can the fantasy of “reality television” be traversed?

abuse; ego ideal; Lacan; language

This paper employs Lacanian theories of language and temporality in order to dissect the workings of emotional abuse. Because emotional abuse varies greatly and can be difficult to describe, this paper attempts to discern the internal mechanisms that allow abuse to function: specifically, how the abused partner is trapped by the linguistic and emotive techniques of the abuser. Lacanian psychoanalysis can help show how the internal dynamic of abuse works, and how it repeats itself through the continuous immobilization of the abused partner.

Lacan; Žižek; cinema; Real; gaze

This paper is part of a wider project that brings together psychoanalysis and film by focusing on the most disruptive and potentially subversive Lacanian notion, that of the Real. My work explores the dialectical relationship between film as a process of symbolic signification and the unconscious/Real underside that it produces, arguing that only by attempting to read the traces of unconscious desire secreted by film can we encroach upon its “truth”. The key cinematic concepts of editing, suture and gaze are here re-assessed through Lacanian theory, while their theoretical and political potential is measured against the work of Italian directors Michelangelo Antonioni and Pier Paolo Pasolini.

In this essay, I argue that it is in the cultural domain of science fiction that social desires repressed in politics and economics are still proposed and enjoyed. Specifically, I consider science fictional attempts to imagine non-capitalist futures that are qualitatively better than our present. Gilbert Cole  

The domestic issue that makes the most noise at this moment in our country's history is the “culture war” over homosexuality. In an article in The New York Times Magazine (Shorto, 2005), it is argued that the question of “gay marriage” is not really about marriage at all, but about regarding homosexuality as a disease that must be fought. The argument is often mounted in terms of spiritual belief. Empirical data, appeals to an empathic understanding of other people's points of view, the expert positions of nationally recognized medical, psychological and educational organizations - in fact any kind of reasoned argument - cannot stand in the face of the certainty of fixed, spiritual belief. The hostility toward those who are unconventional, re-framed as Christian Love by those who work to make sure that lesbian and gay families cannot enjoy the civil rights that straight people do, has become so effective that the issue of gay marriage has been referred to as “the new abortion” (Shorto, 2005, p 37).

Into this tense environment comes this important, necessary book, and one that is filled with tensions of its own. The first tension is expressed in the punning title. Only very recently have same sex couples and families been able to stake a claim for the rights that make up the conventions that heterosexual couples and families take for granted as the unexceptional ground for their lives. Of course, lesbians and gay men have lived in familial structures for as long as the term “homosexual” has been a meaningful descriptor; and before there was such a thing as the “homosexual,” same-sex affectional ties and familial groupings have been a part of human society. Nonetheless, the ways those living in these groupings found to accommodate their exclusion from convention have largely escaped notice and documentation. For lesbians and gay men, the experience of being barred from the conventional facts of life was often both the occasion for a creative accommodation to a hostile world and the reason for a particular constructed “identity.” So to announce in the title of a book of psychoanalytic thinking about same-sex couples and families that convention is to be “uncoupled” is to invite attention to what is most often transparent but required for the standard operations of living. Doing so increases tension.

class; work; thirdness; body

To begin to conceptualize class from a relational perspective, the author proposes that we consider how material relations that color interpersonal relations are absorbed into the psyche and the body. The term “class unconscious” is used to describe a kind of “thirdness”: the child's intersubjective communication with both the maternal and paternal working body. Stein's writing on the “enigmatic signifier” is revisited to describe that part of the parental body that arouses implicit then explicit awareness of the material world of work and class. The author argues that a relational theory of the subject must account for the infiltration of “objective” political phenomena into “subjective” experience. Clinical and autobiographical material illustrate the dynamics of the class unconscious in the transference.

film; testimony; temporality; full speech

This essay interrogates the relation between psychoanalysis, detection and testimony, arguing that psychoanalysis can help us envision the time of testimony as the time of creative repetition - what will be called, following Jacques Lacan, remembrance in the future anterior - only after it critically engages its own relationship to the trial and the model of juridical witnessing to which all witnessing is often assimilated. This paper combines psychoanalysis with socio-cultural theory in order to illuminate the vicissitudes of romantic love. Contemporary sociological theory argues that we are witnessing a new discourse of intimacy in popular culture and in everyday narratives of love and relationships. In a postmodern age, the need for or belief in romantic love might seem unreconstructed and naive, but romantic love retains a compelling hold in contemporary culture and psychoanalysis can help to explain why. This paper demonstrates the need for a socio-psychoanalytic analysis of love ideals and love talk via case material from two female interviewees from different generations and it will discuss what romantic love means for them. It will argue that there is a complex interaction between one's psychic and social self, and demonstrate that it is by analysing this dynamic interplay that we can understand why romantic love is desired and deconstructed in one case, but remains decathected and uninterrogated in the other.

Current influential attempts to bring together psychoanalysis and Marxism turn on the question of how to critique and move beyond capitalism without reverting to a utopian notion of communism. Taking this question seriously, the article explores the implications of psychoanalytic categories such as the real, fantasy, jouissance, and the formulae of sexuation, for Marxian economics and politics. Mark Borg PHD

Mark Borg

156 Fifth Avenue, Suite 725, NewYork, NY 10010, USA
E-mail: OEDTREX@aol.com

Mark Borg   Community/clinical psychologist and interpersonal psychoanalyst who is affiliated with the William Alanson White Institute. He is co-founder and principal partner of the Community Consulting Group, which is a community revitalization organization. He lives and practices in New York City.
palliative care; liberal individualism; interpersonal psychoanalysis; categorical scapegoat; community character; enactment

Enactments of palliative care entail an excess of dissociated pain and anxiety that conforms with the unconscious injunction of our liberal individualist society to “Be Well”. In this paper, I suggest that palliative care rituals serve as society-level unconscious defenses that Westerners use to ward off any form of emotional discomfort. This paper follows a patient, starting with a “zombie” dream presented in her initial session, through the first 6 years of her psychoanalytic treatment as she moves through this palliative care system.

It does not seem as if Augustine's conception of evil as the privation or absence of goodness is adequate to account for the horrors of the 20th century. Whether this is true depends on how we interpret “privation.” Drawing on Melanie Klein and Wilfred Bion, I argue that the privation of goodness may be seen not merely as the absence of goodness, but as the active destruction of goodness, its intentional deprivation. This, it turns out, is enough to make sense of Hannah Arendt's otherwise confusing concept of the banality of evil. Making sense of her concept does not, however, make it right.

Ricardo Ainslie  

For those interested in psychoanalytic reflections on the pernicious forces of racism, homophobia, and misogyny, this book is an invaluable resource. The conceptual driving force behind this collection is Moss's formulation of the psychodynamic processes via which individual conflictual desires are subject to an especially dangerous transformation: from “I want” to “we hate.” One of Moss's most interesting observations emphasizes the fact that we do not hate as isolated individuals, rather, we hate as a group (“in the first person plural”). Such hatred has a psychologically binding impact and becomes an essential constituent of identity by serving as a means of linkage to others. We enlist hatreds in a struggle for self-definition, Moss tells us, and the mechanism proceeds in two directions simultaneously: via a disidentification from the objects that stir anxiety-provoking and disavowed desires, and via identification with others who provide a sense of solidarity through a shared hatred.

Hating in the First Person Plural is organized into four sections.

On Racism: Four chapters comprise this section of the book (in addition to Moss's excellent introduction), with contributions by Maurice Apprey (“Repairing History: Reworking Transgenerational Trauma”), Alan Bass (“Historical and Unconscious Trauma: Racism and Psychoanalysis”), David Marriott (“The derived Life of Fiction: Race, Childhood, and Culture”), and E. Victor Wolfenstein (“Race, Rage, and Oedipus in Ralph Ellison's Invisible Man”).

Apprey's chapter theorizes that trauma is transmitted from one generation to the next and analyzes the implications of such “deferred” history as it contributes to an aggrieved group remaining “disfigured, dehumanized and traumatized as a people” (p 13). This is the basis for a transgenerational haunting that is unacknowledged, but like all unconscious processes, highly potent and influential.

Alan Bass is also interested in how traumatizing history becomes transmitted, and how the victim of racism is affected by the racist's unconscious fantasy, transmitting this encrypted perception to the next generation. Bass helps us see the ways in which the absence of psychoanalytic theorizing on the effects of racism has hindered therapeutic praxis.

A family-oriented PG-13 film of the 1990s illustrates an argument for a more grounded sense of developmental trauma and social antagonism in studies of ideological fantasy. The paper argues that Hollywood films are often most ideological when production of the romantic couple is tied to resolving the split between domestic and commercial spaces. The analysis suggests that Freud's views of the intimate relation and society can serve as a corrective to overly reified and socially detached uses of Lacan in film studies.
